## Overview

The Czechs (Czech: *Češi*; singular masculine: *Čech*; singular feminine: *Češka*), or Czech people (*Český lid*), are a West Slavic ethnic group and nation native to the Czech Republic in Central Europe. They share a common culture, ancestry, history, and speak the Czech language. Czechs live in the three historical lands of Bohemia, Moravia, and Czech Silesia, which make up the modern Czech Republic, now divided into 14 administrative regions. The Czech language is spoken by approximately 12 million people around the world. Czech culture developed through interaction among Slavic, Celtic, Germanic, and neighbouring Slovak populations. Its documented cultural fields include music, literature, visual arts, film, religious traditions, regional dialects, and the historical revival of Czech language, culture, and national identity.

## Material culture

### Architecture

The sources identify Prague Castle, constructed in 880 by Prince Bořivoj, founder of the Přemyslid dynasty, and the city of Prague.

## Music & performance

Czech music had significant pieces by the 11th century. The development of Czech artificial music advanced at the end of the Renaissance and during the early Baroque era, including the work of Adam Václav Michna z Otradovic. The sources describe genuine folk music as an influence that helped determine the development of Czech music and remained a sign of the work of composers in later periods.

Named composers include Jan Dismas Zelenka and Josef Mysliveček in the Baroque, Bedřich Smetana and Antonín Dvořák in Romanticism, and Leoš Janáček, Bohuslav Martinů, Josef Suk, Petr Eben, and Miloslav Kabeláč in modern and contemporary classical music. Jan Václav Antonín Stamic contributed to the creation of Classicism in music and founded the Mannheim school. Antonín Rejcha’s experiments prefigured new compositional techniques in the 19th century, while Alois Hába contributed to microtonal music in the 20th century.

Karel Slavíček was a Jesuit missionary, scientist, and sinologist who was introduced to the Kangxi Emperor on 3 February 1717, in Beijing. The emperor employed him as court musician, and Slavíček was a Spinet player. The rock band The Plastic People of the Universe played an important part in the underground movement during the communist regime.

## Dance & theatre

The sources identify Jiří Kylián as an important ballet choreographer and mention theatrical avant-garde figures including Jan Werich, Jiří Voskovec, and Emil František Burian. They also describe film and puppet-film figures such as Zdeněk Miler, Karel Zeman, and Jiří Trnka.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe the Czech National Revival of the 18th and 19th centuries as a movement focused on reviving Czech language, culture, and national identity. Czech culture involves saints including St. Wenceslaus (Václav), patron of the Czech nation; St. John of Nepomuk (Jan Nepomucký); St. Adalbert (Vojtěch); Saint Procopius; and St. Agnes of Bohemia (Anežka Česká). Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel of Prague, a 16th Century scholar, is also described as part of the country’s religious legacy.

The sources record the founding legend of Forefather Čech, who brought the tribe of Czechs into its land, and a popular account in which the Slavs came with Forefather Čech, who settled at the Říp Mountain.

## Oral tradition & literature

According to mythology and legend, Forefather Čech was the founding father of the Czech people and brought the tribe of Czechs into its land. Another popular myth says that the Slavs came with Forefather Čech, who settled at the Říp Mountain. The sources also preserve a legend that the ethnonym *Čech* derives from the leader Čech, who brought the tribe to Bohemia, although the exact etymology is uncertain.

Czech literature includes Kosmas, Božena Němcová, Karel Čapek, Jaroslav Hašek, Jan Neruda, Franz Kafka, Bohumil Hrabal, Viktor Dyk, Pavel Kohout, Alois Jirásek, Josef Škvorecký, Karel Jaromír Erben, Jiří Wolker, Karel Hynek Mácha, Vítězslav Nezval, Arnošt Lustig, Jaroslav Vrchlický, Karel Havlíček Borovský, Ivan Klíma, Egon Erwin Kisch, Vladimír Holan, Julius Zeyer, and Svatopluk Čech. Jaroslav Seifert was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature for his poetry, while Božena Němcová became a cultural icon through her book *Babička* (*The Grandmother*).

## Language & religion

Czech belongs to the West Slavic subgroup of the larger Slavic ethno-linguistical group. The Czech–Slovak languages form a dialect continuum rather than being two clearly distinct languages. Local dialects include Central Bohemian, the Chod dialect, Moravian dialects, and Cieszyn Silesian. Czech is spoken by approximately 12 million people around the world.

The sources describe the Christianization of Great Moravia and the crucial role of the Byzantine mission of Cyril and Methodius. Czech culture involves saints including St. Wenceslaus, St. John of Nepomuk, St. Adalbert, Saint Procopius, and St. Agnes of Bohemia. They also identify Jan Hus as a religious reformist from the 15th century and spiritual father of the Hussite Movement, and Jan Žižka and Prokop the Great as leaders of the hussite army. Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel of Prague is described as part of the country’s Jewish religious legacy.
